H("B. Detailed discussion", 2)

H("Issue 1 — § 6.1 Mandatory Initial Data Exchange (Critical)", 3)
P("**What it says.** Within 30 days of the Effective Date each party must deliver: (a) three years of audited financials; (b) current product-line revenue, cost and margin data; (c) customer lists with annualized revenue by customer; (d) production capacity and utilization by facility; (e) current pricing schedules and standard discount matrices; and (f) five-year strategic plans including planned capacity expansions and new product launches — and must use commercially reasonable efforts to ensure accuracy and completeness.", align="j")
P("**Why it is a problem.** Items (b) through (f) are, almost verbatim, the categories the Market Overview identifies as the most competitively sensitive in this industry (§ 4.2: discount and rebate matrices are “among the most closely guarded competitive secrets”; § 7, rec. 3: current pricing, customer-specific data, discount structures, capacity utilization and forward-looking strategy “should not be shared beyond what is demonstrably required”). They relate to the parties’ existing virgin carbon fiber businesses, which by design will remain independent and competing (Team Memo § I). The JV is a greenfield rCF business in which neither party has a product, customers or prices. There is no evident need for either party to see the other’s current customer-by-customer revenue, discount matrices or plant utilization in order to evaluate an rCF JV; the agencies would be expected to ask exactly that question. The *mandatory* nature of the obligation is itself aggravating: it converts the exchange from an evaluation-driven, need-based process into an affirmative contractual commitment by two leading competitors to swap pricing and output data, and it removes Pinnacle’s ability to decline on antitrust grounds. Timing (within 30 days) also coincides with the Northwind award (Issue 7).", align="j")
P("**Note on Pinnacle’s own requests.** The Team Memo (§§ IV–V) lists essentially the same categories as information Pinnacle intends to request and to provide, and directs the team to begin assembling Pinnacle’s current pricing schedules and customer lists for disclosure. The § 6.1 list appears to mirror that list. Pinnacle should recalibrate its own requests at the same time it pushes back on § 6.1, so that its negotiating position is consistent (see Section IX).", align="j")
P("**Recommended revision.** Delete § 6.1 and replace with:")
Q("“6.1 *Information Requests.* Any exchange of information under this Agreement shall be voluntary and limited to information that is reasonably necessary for the Permitted Purpose. Requests shall be made in writing through the Parties’ designated legal coordinators and shall be reviewed by each Party’s antitrust counsel before any information is provided. Nothing in this Agreement obligates either Party to provide any particular information, and either Party may decline to provide, or may provide only in redacted, aggregated, historical or summary form, any information that it or its counsel determines in good faith to be Competitively Sensitive Information or otherwise inappropriate to share between competitors. All Competitively Sensitive Information shall be provided only in accordance with the Clean Team Agreement and the Antitrust Compliance Annex attached as Exhibits A and B.”")
P("Pinnacle should propose a staged request list focused on rCF: Phase 1 (non-sensitive) — rCF technology, pilot programs and IP relevant to rCF; feedstock sources and recycling processes; JV capital requirements, site options and governance; audited financial statements (to assess financial capability as a JV partner). Phase 2 (Clean Team only) — cost inputs relevant to rCF modeling, presented as ranges or indexed values; anticipated contributions of personnel or assets to the JV. Customer-specific pricing, discount and rebate matrices, customer lists with revenue by customer, open bid information and existing-product strategic plans should be excluded entirely; if a demonstrated need emerges (e.g., to model JV demand), it should be met by an independent consultant producing aggregated, anonymized outputs, or by data at least several months old and aggregated across customers.", align="j")

H("Issue 2 — § 6.2 Quarterly Updates (Critical)", 3)
P("Requiring both parties to refresh every § 6.1 category within 15 business days of each fiscal quarter-end for the 18-month (and auto-renewing) Evaluation Period creates a standing, periodic exchange of current price, cost, customer and capacity data between the #1 and #3 producers. Regular, current, disaggregated exchanges are the pattern condemned in *Container Corp.* and the core concern of recent DOJ information-exchange enforcement. No evaluation of a JV targeted for signing by June 30, 2025 requires quarterly refreshes of the parents’ existing-business pricing. **Recommendation:** delete § 6.2 in its entirety. Any updates should be requested case by case under revised § 6.1.", align="j")

H("Issue 3 — §§ 1.6 and 4.1 Representatives; Absence of Clean Team (Critical)", 3)
P("“Representatives” includes all directors, officers, employees, agents, advisors, consultants and affiliates, and § 4.1 allows disclosure to any of them, with each party “solely responsible for determining which of its Representatives shall receive access to particular categories of Confidential Information.” There is no need-to-know requirement, no clean team, no restriction on disclosure to sales and pricing personnel, and no requirement that Representatives sign anything. As you correctly identified, Mr. Hecht (VP Sales) and Ms. Vasquez (VP Strategic Pricing), both involved day-to-day in competitive pricing and customer negotiations, would receive Lakeshore’s pricing, customer and cost data and then return to Pinnacle’s pricing decisions — and the same would be true of Lakeshore’s commercial staff with Pinnacle’s data. Beyond the § 1 risk, this exposes Pinnacle to misappropriation claims and taints its future pricing decisions with an inference of reliance on Lakeshore data.", align="j")
P("**Recommended revision.** Revise § 1.6 to define Representatives as those “who have a need to know such information for the Permitted Purpose,” and replace § 4.1 with:")
Q("“4.1 *Disclosure to Representatives.* The Receiving Party may disclose Confidential Information only to those of its Representatives who need to know such information for the Permitted Purpose, who have been informed of its confidential nature and who are bound by obligations of confidentiality no less protective than those herein. Notwithstanding the foregoing, Competitively Sensitive Information (as defined in Section 2.4) may be disclosed only to (i) the Receiving Party’s outside legal counsel and outside consultants and economic advisers engaged for the Permitted Purpose and (ii) members of the Receiving Party’s Clean Team, in each case in accordance with the Clean Team Agreement attached as Exhibit A. No Competitively Sensitive Information shall be disclosed to any individual with direct responsibility for pricing, sales, marketing, bidding, customer negotiations or capacity planning for products that compete with products of the Disclosing Party.”")
P("Add new § 2.4 defining “Competitively Sensitive Information” (see Appendix B) and require written acknowledgments from Clean Team members.", align="j")

H("Issue 4 — §§ 1.7, 5.3 and 8.3(ii) Residuals Clause (Critical)", 3)
P("Section 5.3 provides that nothing restricts either party from using “in its business activities” any Residual Information retained in the unaided memories of Representatives, and § 8.3(ii) exempts residuals from return or destruction. Combined with § 4.1’s unrestricted access, this would permit pricing and sales personnel to use whatever they remember of a competitor’s pricing, discount structures, customer volumes and strategic plans in competing against that competitor. Residuals clauses are sometimes accepted in technology licensing for general skills and know-how; between horizontal competitors exchanging commercial data, they function as a license to use the competitor’s information competitively and would be strong evidence that the exchange was not confined to the transaction. The clause also substantially undercuts the confidentiality protection for Pinnacle’s own data in the hands of a larger rival and would undermine any trade secret claim. The IP carve-out in the last sentence of § 5.3 is not a meaningful limitation. **Recommendation:** delete § 1.7, § 5.3 and clause (ii) of § 8.3 in their entirety. Do not accept a narrowed version; at most, a statement that general skills and experience of individuals not derived from Competitively Sensitive Information are unaffected.", align="j")

H("Issue 5 — § 9.3 Mutual Release and Limitation on Claims (Critical)", 3)
P("Each party agrees not to assert any claim “arising from or related to the exchange of Confidential Information hereunder, including … any claim based on antitrust or competition law, unfair competition, tortious interference, or misappropriation,” other than for willful and material breach of §§ 2–6. This is problematic on four levels:", align="j")
B("**Unenforceability.** A prospective waiver of federal antitrust remedies is very likely void as against public policy. *Mitsubishi Motors Corp. v. Soler Chrysler-Plymouth, Inc.*, 473 U.S. 614, 637 n.19 (1985) (Court would have “little hesitation in condemning” an agreement operating as a prospective waiver of the right to pursue antitrust remedies). Including an unenforceable clause provides no protection.")
B("**It does not reach the parties who matter.** The DOJ, FTC, state attorneys general and customers (e.g., automotive OEMs or Northwind, who could seek treble damages under Clayton Act § 4) are not bound.")
B("**It harms Pinnacle.** As the smaller party disclosing to the market leader, Pinnacle would waive its own antitrust, unfair competition and misappropriation claims if Lakeshore misuses Pinnacle data (e.g., to target Pinnacle accounts), leaving only a narrow “willful and material” breach claim.")
B("**It is a damaging document.** A clause in which competitors mutually release antitrust claims arising from their information exchange would be read by an investigator or jury as evidence that the parties anticipated the exchange could be anticompetitive. It would be among the first provisions highlighted in any investigation.")
P("**Recommendation:** delete § 9.3 in its entirety. Replace, if anything, with the Antitrust Compliance clause in Issue 14 and clarify in § 11.2 that the limitation on reliance does not limit liability for breach of this Agreement or misuse of Confidential Information.", align="j")

H("Issue 6 — § 6.3 Monthly Executive Meetings (Critical)", 3)
P("The parties must designate senior executives to meet “no less frequently than monthly” to discuss the evaluation “and matters of mutual interest,” and either party may add any Representatives. Recurring, unstructured meetings among competing senior executives are a well-recognized antitrust hazard: they create opportunity and, in hindsight, inference of agreement. “Matters of mutual interest” between the #1 and #3 competitors has no limiting principle and could readily be characterized as cover for discussing pricing, customers, capacity or the Northwind bid. **Recommendation:** replace § 6.3 with:", align="j")
Q("“6.3 *Meetings.* Meetings between the Parties’ Representatives concerning the Transaction shall be held as reasonably required for the Permitted Purpose and shall be limited to matters directly related to the evaluation and negotiation of the Transaction. Each meeting shall proceed under a written agenda circulated in advance and reviewed by each Party’s legal counsel; legal counsel for each Party shall be entitled to attend, and counsel shall attend any meeting at which Competitively Sensitive Information may be discussed. Minutes shall be prepared and retained. Representatives shall not discuss current or future prices, pricing strategies, discounts, bids, terms of sale, customers or suppliers (other than in respect of the JV business as permitted by the Antitrust Compliance Annex), capacity, output, wages or other terms of employment, or any other competitively sensitive matter relating to the Parties’ respective businesses outside the Transaction. Any participant may terminate a discussion that he or she believes to be inappropriate, and such termination shall be recorded in the minutes.”")

H("Issue 7 — The Northwind Aerospace Bid (Critical; not addressed by the draft)", 3)
P("Pinnacle and Lakeshore are rival bidders on a three-year Northwind supply contract (~$22 million/year), with award expected in February 2025. If the NDA is signed January 31, § 6.1 would require the delivery of current pricing schedules, discount matrices and customer revenue data by about March 2, 2025 — during or immediately around the award decision. Lakeshore’s receipt of Pinnacle’s current aerospace pricing (or vice versa) while the bid is open, or while best-and-final or post-award negotiations remain possible, could be characterized as facilitating bid rigging (a per se, criminal offense) and would at minimum create a damaging evidentiary record if the losing bidder or Northwind later questioned the outcome. Aerospace pricing has no relevance to an automotive rCF JV.", align="j")
P("**Recommendations:**")
B("Add an express blackout: no Party shall request, disclose or discuss any information concerning the Northwind procurement or any other pending or anticipated bid, tender or RFQ in which both Parties are or may be participants, at any time, including after award.")
B("No Phase 2 (Clean Team) commercial or cost data should be exchanged before the Northwind award is announced and any best-and-final or negotiation round has concluded; Phase 1 technical rCF work can proceed.")
B("Instruct the Pinnacle Northwind bid team (in writing) that it must not receive any Project Meridian information, and confirm that no Northwind bid team member is on the Clean Team.")
B("Each party should confirm in writing (Annex) that its Northwind bid was and will be determined independently.")
B("If Pinnacle learns of any communication between the parties concerning Northwind, it should contact us immediately.")

H("Issue 8 — §§ 1.8 and 3.1 Transaction / Permitted Purpose (High)", 3)
P("“Transaction” and “Permitted Purpose” cover “any joint venture, merger, acquisition, licensing arrangement, or other business combination,” and include “consummating” the Transaction and “integration planning activities.” As your email notes, this is an M&A form. It is inconsistent with the Board-approved scope — a JV focused “exclusively” on rCF, with no consolidation of existing operations — and it broadens the legitimate need for information to whole-company merger diligence, which the parties would then use to justify existing-business data requests. “Consummating” and “integration planning” invite pre-closing implementation and coordination (gun-jumping). The definition is also duplicated (once in § 1.8 and again in § 3.1), which should be cleaned up.", align="j")
P("**Recommended revision:**")
Q("“‘Transaction’ means a potential joint venture between the Parties limited to the research, development, manufacture and commercialization of recycled carbon fiber products for automotive lightweighting applications (the ‘JV Business’). ‘Permitted Purpose’ means the evaluation and negotiation of the Transaction and, to the extent permitted by the Clean Team Agreement and Antitrust Compliance Annex, planning for the formation and operation of the JV Business following execution of definitive agreements. The Permitted Purpose does not include the implementation of any aspect of the Transaction, or any coordination of the Parties’ respective businesses, prior to the consummation of the Transaction and receipt of any required regulatory clearances.”")

H("Issue 9 — § 2.1 Confidential Information Definition (High)", 3)
P("From a confidentiality standpoint a broad definition is protective, and Pinnacle should not want its own information left unprotected merely because it falls outside rCF. The antitrust risk is not that the definition protects too much, but that §§ 2.1, 6.1 and 4.1 together presuppose and authorize the exchange of all of it, without any differentiated handling. Items (c) pricing, (d) customer lists/contracts/pricing/volumes, (e) supplier and raw material costs, (f) production volumes, capacity utilization and plant-level costs, (g) product roadmaps, (h) compensation data and (i) sales volumes and market share are all competitively sensitive. **Recommendation:** keep a broad definition of Confidential Information for protection purposes, but (i) add a defined subcategory of Competitively Sensitive Information (Appendix B, § 2.4) subject to clean team handling, (ii) require CSI to be labeled “CLEAN TEAM ONLY” or “OUTSIDE COUNSEL ONLY” (while preserving protection for unlabeled information), and (iii) add a statement that inclusion of a category in the definition does not imply that such information will be or should be exchanged. Also expressly cover information disclosed prior to the Effective Date in connection with Project Meridian, so any earlier executive-level discussions are protected.", align="j")

H("Issue 10 — § 2.1(h) Employee Compensation Data (High)", 3)
P("Pinnacle and Lakeshore compete for engineers, technicians and plant workers. The exchange of compensation and headcount data between competing employers carries wage-fixing risk that the agencies treat seriously (2025 Worker Guidelines; 2016 HR Guidance), and the Team Memo specifically contemplates exchanging “compensation benchmarking data for relevant technical and operational roles.” **Recommendation:** no exchange of individual or role-level compensation data between the parties. If JV staffing economics require it, use an independent compensation consultant to prepare aggregated, anonymized JV staffing cost assumptions, or exchange only aggregated data for specific individuals proposed to be seconded to the JV, through the Clean Team.", align="j")

H("Issue 11 — § 8.1 Term and Automatic Renewal (High)", 3)
P("The 18-month Initial Term automatically renews for successive 12-month periods unless either party gives 90 days’ notice. Because the term drives the Evaluation Period, the § 6.2 quarterly exchanges, the § 6.3 meetings and the start of the 24-month non-solicit and standstill tails, auto-renewal could perpetuate a recurring competitor data exchange indefinitely if neither party remembers to give notice. Prolonged exchange untethered to a live deal is hard to justify. **Recommendation:** fixed term of 12 months (comfortably covering the June 30, 2025 definitive agreement target), terminable by either party on written notice and terminating automatically on execution of definitive agreements (which will contain their own provisions) or termination of discussions; any extension only by written agreement. The five-year confidentiality survival in § 8.2 is appropriate and protective and may be retained; consider extending trade-secret protection for as long as the information remains a trade secret.", align="j")

H("Issue 12 — § 7.1 Employee Non-Solicitation (High)", 3)
P("Section 7.1 bars soliciting, recruiting, **or hiring** any employee (or former employee within six months) who became known in connection with the Transaction, for the term (auto-renewing) plus 24 months. A non-solicit ancillary to a legitimate JV evaluation is defensible if reasonably necessary and narrowly tailored, but this one has features that increase the risk of it being characterized as a no-poach agreement: (i) the “hire” prohibition operates as a no-hire restraint even for employees who apply on their own; (ii) its duration is open-ended because it runs from an auto-renewing term; (iii) “became known … in connection with the Transaction” is loosely defined and could sweep in large numbers of employees; and (iv) it covers former employees. **Recommendation:**", align="j")
Q("“7.1 For a period of twelve (12) months from the Effective Date, neither Party shall, directly or indirectly, solicit for employment any officer or employee of the other Party with whom it first had contact, or of whom it first became aware, through the evaluation of the Transaction; provided that this Section 7.1 shall not restrict (a) general solicitations (including through search firms) not specifically directed at such persons, or hiring persons who respond thereto, (b) soliciting or hiring any person who first contacts the soliciting Party on his or her own initiative, or (c) soliciting or hiring any person whose employment was terminated by the other Party.”")
P("We also recommend confirming whether the parties have Canadian employees, given Canada’s criminal no-poach provision.", align="j")

H("Issue 13 — § 5.2 Exclusions; Absence of Compelled/Regulatory Disclosure Clause (Medium)", 3)
P("The exclusions omit two standard carve-outs that have particular antitrust importance between competitors: (i) information **independently developed** without use of the other’s Confidential Information, and (ii) information **received from a third party** without a duty of confidentiality. Without them, Pinnacle could face claims that its own independently developed pricing, product or rCF strategy was “derived from” Lakeshore information, which chills independent competition. The written-records requirement in § 5.2(b) should be relaxed to “as shown by competent evidence.” Separately, the NDA has no provision permitting disclosure required by law or requested by a governmental authority. Pinnacle must be free to respond to an HSR filing requirement, a Second Request, a civil investigative demand, a subpoena or an informal agency inquiry without breaching the NDA, and should not be required to give the other party advance notice of a confidential governmental antitrust inquiry where that is prohibited or inappropriate. See Appendix B, §§ 5.2 and 5.4.", align="j")

H("Issue 14 — §§ 12.9, 12.10 No Independence or Antitrust Compliance Clause (Medium)", 3)
P("The general “Compliance with Law” clause in § 12.10 is not sufficient. The NDA should affirmatively record that (i) the parties are and will remain independent competitors; (ii) nothing in the Agreement requires or permits any agreement on prices, output, customers, territories, bids, wages or other competitive matters; (iii) each party will continue to make its own competitive decisions independently; (iv) either party may decline to provide information on antitrust grounds; and (v) the Clean Team Agreement and Antitrust Compliance Annex control in case of conflict. This clause is useful both as a behavioral guide and as contemporaneous evidence of the parties’ intent. See Appendix B, § 12.11.", align="j")

H("Issue 15 — § 8.3 Return or Destruction (Medium)", 3)
P("Section 8.3 allows retention of one archival copy without specifying who holds it, and exempts Residual Information. **Recommendation:** archival copies (and copies retained on automatic backup systems) to be held only by the legal department or outside counsel and accessible only for compliance and enforcement; delete clause (ii); require Clean Team materials and Derivative Materials containing CSI to be destroyed with written certification by a Clean Team member and counsel; confirm the obligation survives.", align="j")

H("Issues 16–20 — Lower-severity points", 3)
B("**§ 4.3 Information Access Log (retain and strengthen).** This is a positive feature that supports compliance and should be retained. Expand it to record, for CSI, each Clean Team member granted access, the date and the materials accessed, and integrate it with the virtual data room’s access logs.")
B("**§ 2.3 Derivative Materials.** Appropriate as a protective matter. Add a mechanism under which Clean Team members and outside advisers may prepare summaries that aggregate or sanitize CSI and, once cleared by outside antitrust counsel for the producing party, share them with the broader evaluation team.")
B("**§ 7.2 Standstill.** Standstills raise limited antitrust risk. Clarify that clause (a) does not restrict ordinary-course purchases of products or assets; shorten the tail to 12 months; add a customary fall-away if a third party announces or makes an offer for a party; and confirm whether either party has registered securities (§ 13(d) references suggest a public-company form; Lakeshore is an LLC).")
B("**§§ 9.1, 9.2 Governing Law/Arbitration.** Not antitrust issues as such, but: the National Arbitration Forum withdrew from consumer arbitration in 2009 and its suitability as an administrator for a commercial dispute should be confirmed — we recommend AAA (Commercial Rules) or JAMS; preserve the right to seek interim injunctive relief in court (consistent with § 10.1); and consider Delaware law (both parties are Delaware entities) as a neutral alternative to Ohio, Lakeshore’s home state.")
B("**§ 12.1 Entire Agreement.** Ensure the Clean Team Agreement and Antitrust Compliance Annex are attached as exhibits, are expressly incorporated, prevail over any conflicting NDA provision, and survive termination.")

H("B. Detailed discussion", 2)

H("Issue 1 — § 6.1 Mandatory Initial Data Exchange (Critical)", 3)
P("**What it says.** Within 30 days of the Effective Date each party must deliver: (a) three years of audited financials; (b) current product-line revenue, cost and margin data; (c) customer lists with annualized revenue by customer; (d) production capacity and utilization by facility; (e) current pricing schedules and standard discount matrices; and (f) five-year strategic plans including planned capacity expansions and new product launches — and must use commercially reasonable efforts to ensure accuracy and completeness.", align="j")
P("**Why it is a problem.** Items (b) through (f) are, almost verbatim, the categories the Market Overview identifies as the most competitively sensitive in this industry (§ 4.2: discount and rebate matrices are “among the most closely guarded competitive secrets”; § 7, rec. 3: current pricing, customer-specific data, discount structures, capacity utilization and forward-looking strategy “should not be shared beyond what is demonstrably required”). They relate to the parties’ existing virgin carbon fiber businesses, which by design will remain independent and competing (Team Memo § I). The JV is a greenfield rCF business in which neither party has a product, customers or prices. There is no evident need for either party to see the other’s current customer-by-customer revenue, discount matrices or plant utilization in order to evaluate an rCF JV; the agencies would be expected to ask exactly that question. The *mandatory* nature of the obligation is itself aggravating: it converts the exchange from an evaluation-driven, need-based process into an affirmative contractual commitment by two leading competitors to swap pricing and output data, and it removes Pinnacle’s ability to decline on antitrust grounds. Timing (within 30 days) also coincides with the Northwind award (Issue 7).", align="j")
P("**Note on Pinnacle’s own requests.** The Team Memo (§§ IV–V) lists essentially the same categories as information Pinnacle intends to request and to provide, and directs the team to begin assembling Pinnacle’s current pricing schedules and customer lists for disclosure. The § 6.1 list appears to mirror that list. Pinnacle should recalibrate its own requests at the same time it pushes back on § 6.1, so that its negotiating position is consistent (see Section IX).", align="j")
P("**Recommended revision.** Delete § 6.1 and replace with:")
Q("“6.1 *Information Requests.* Any exchange of information under this Agreement shall be voluntary and limited to information that is reasonably necessary for the Permitted Purpose. Requests shall be made in writing through the Parties’ designated legal coordinators and shall be reviewed by each Party’s antitrust counsel before any information is provided. Nothing in this Agreement obligates either Party to provide any particular information, and either Party may decline to provide, or may provide only in redacted, aggregated, historical or summary form, any information that it or its counsel determines in good faith to be Competitively Sensitive Information or otherwise inappropriate to share between competitors. All Competitively Sensitive Information shall be provided only in accordance with the Clean Team Agreement and the Antitrust Compliance Annex attached as Exhibits A and B.”")
P("Pinnacle should propose a staged request list focused on rCF: Phase 1 (non-sensitive) — rCF technology, pilot programs and IP relevant to rCF; feedstock sources and recycling processes; JV capital requirements, site options and governance; audited financial statements (to assess financial capability as a JV partner). Phase 2 (Clean Team only) — cost inputs relevant to rCF modeling, presented as ranges or indexed values; anticipated contributions of personnel or assets to the JV. Customer-specific pricing, discount and rebate matrices, customer lists with revenue by customer, open bid information and existing-product strategic plans should be excluded entirely; if a demonstrated need emerges (e.g., to model JV demand), it should be met by an independent consultant producing aggregated, anonymized outputs, or by data at least several months old and aggregated across customers.", align="j")

H("Issue 2 — § 6.2 Quarterly Updates (Critical)", 3)
P("Requiring both parties to refresh every § 6.1 category within 15 business days of each fiscal quarter-end for the 18-month (and auto-renewing) Evaluation Period creates a standing, periodic exchange of current price, cost, customer and capacity data between the #1 and #3 producers. Regular, current, disaggregated exchanges are the pattern condemned in *Container Corp.* and the core concern of recent DOJ information-exchange enforcement. No evaluation of a JV targeted for signing by June 30, 2025 requires quarterly refreshes of the parents’ existing-business pricing. **Recommendation:** delete § 6.2 in its entirety. Any updates should be requested case by case under revised § 6.1.", align="j")

H("Issue 3 — §§ 1.6 and 4.1 Representatives; Absence of Clean Team (Critical)", 3)
P("“Representatives” includes all directors, officers, employees, agents, advisors, consultants and affiliates, and § 4.1 allows disclosure to any of them, with each party “solely responsible for determining which of its Representatives shall receive access to particular categories of Confidential Information.” There is no need-to-know requirement, no clean team, no restriction on disclosure to sales and pricing personnel, and no requirement that Representatives sign anything. As you correctly identified, Mr. Hecht (VP Sales) and Ms. Vasquez (VP Strategic Pricing), both involved day-to-day in competitive pricing and customer negotiations, would receive Lakeshore’s pricing, customer and cost data and then return to Pinnacle’s pricing decisions — and the same would be true of Lakeshore’s commercial staff with Pinnacle’s data. Beyond the § 1 risk, this exposes Pinnacle to misappropriation claims and taints its future pricing decisions with an inference of reliance on Lakeshore data.", align="j")
P("**Recommended revision.** Revise § 1.6 to define Representatives as those “who have a need to know such information for the Permitted Purpose,” and replace § 4.1 with:")
Q("“4.1 *Disclosure to Representatives.* The Receiving Party may disclose Confidential Information only to those of its Representatives who need to know such information for the Permitted Purpose, who have been informed of its confidential nature and who are bound by obligations of confidentiality no less protective than those herein. Notwithstanding the foregoing, Competitively Sensitive Information (as defined in Section 2.4) may be disclosed only to (i) the Receiving Party’s outside legal counsel and outside consultants and economic advisers engaged for the Permitted Purpose and (ii) members of the Receiving Party’s Clean Team, in each case in accordance with the Clean Team Agreement attached as Exhibit A. No Competitively Sensitive Information shall be disclosed to any individual with direct responsibility for pricing, sales, marketing, bidding, customer negotiations or capacity planning for products that compete with products of the Disclosing Party.”")
P("Add new § 2.4 defining “Competitively Sensitive Information” (see Appendix B) and require written acknowledgments from Clean Team members.", align="j")

H("Issue 4 — §§ 1.7, 5.3 and 8.3(ii) Residuals Clause (Critical)", 3)
P("Section 5.3 provides that nothing restricts either party from using “in its business activities” any Residual Information retained in the unaided memories of Representatives, and § 8.3(ii) exempts residuals from return or destruction. Combined with § 4.1’s unrestricted access, this would permit pricing and sales personnel to use whatever they remember of a competitor’s pricing, discount structures, customer volumes and strategic plans in competing against that competitor. Residuals clauses are sometimes accepted in technology licensing for general skills and know-how; between horizontal competitors exchanging commercial data, they function as a license to use the competitor’s information competitively and would be strong evidence that the exchange was not confined to the transaction. The clause also substantially undercuts the confidentiality protection for Pinnacle’s own data in the hands of a larger rival and would undermine any trade secret claim. The IP carve-out in the last sentence of § 5.3 is not a meaningful limitation. **Recommendation:** delete § 1.7, § 5.3 and clause (ii) of § 8.3 in their entirety. Do not accept a narrowed version; at most, a statement that general skills and experience of individuals not derived from Competitively Sensitive Information are unaffected.", align="j")

H("Issue 5 — § 9.3 Mutual Release and Limitation on Claims (Critical)", 3)
P("Each party agrees not to assert any claim “arising from or related to the exchange of Confidential Information hereunder, including … any claim based on antitrust or competition law, unfair competition, tortious interference, or misappropriation,” other than for willful and material breach of §§ 2–6. This is problematic on four levels:", align="j")
B("**Unenforceability.** A prospective waiver of federal antitrust remedies is very likely void as against public policy. *Mitsubishi Motors Corp. v. Soler Chrysler-Plymouth, Inc.*, 473 U.S. 614, 637 n.19 (1985) (Court would have “little hesitation in condemning” an agreement operating as a prospective waiver of the right to pursue antitrust remedies). Including an unenforceable clause provides no protection.")
B("**It does not reach the parties who matter.** The DOJ, FTC, state attorneys general and customers (e.g., automotive OEMs or Northwind, who could seek treble damages under Clayton Act § 4) are not bound.")
B("**It harms Pinnacle.** As the smaller party disclosing to the market leader, Pinnacle would waive its own antitrust, unfair competition and misappropriation claims if Lakeshore misuses Pinnacle data (e.g., to target Pinnacle accounts), leaving only a narrow “willful and material” breach claim.")
B("**It is a damaging document.** A clause in which competitors mutually release antitrust claims arising from their information exchange would be read by an investigator or jury as evidence that the parties anticipated the exchange could be anticompetitive. It would be among the first provisions highlighted in any investigation.")
P("**Recommendation:** delete § 9.3 in its entirety. Replace, if anything, with the Antitrust Compliance clause in Issue 14 and clarify in § 11.2 that the limitation on reliance does not limit liability for breach of this Agreement or misuse of Confidential Information.", align="j")

H("Issue 6 — § 6.3 Monthly Executive Meetings (Critical)", 3)
P("The parties must designate senior executives to meet “no less frequently than monthly” to discuss the evaluation “and matters of mutual interest,” and either party may add any Representatives. Recurring, unstructured meetings among competing senior executives are a well-recognized antitrust hazard: they create opportunity and, in hindsight, inference of agreement. “Matters of mutual interest” between the #1 and #3 competitors has no limiting principle and could readily be characterized as cover for discussing pricing, customers, capacity or the Northwind bid. **Recommendation:** replace § 6.3 with:", align="j")
Q("“6.3 *Meetings.* Meetings between the Parties’ Representatives concerning the Transaction shall be held as reasonably required for the Permitted Purpose and shall be limited to matters directly related to the evaluation and negotiation of the Transaction. Each meeting shall proceed under a written agenda circulated in advance and reviewed by each Party’s legal counsel; legal counsel for each Party shall be entitled to attend, and counsel shall attend any meeting at which Competitively Sensitive Information may be discussed. Minutes shall be prepared and retained. Representatives shall not discuss current or future prices, pricing strategies, discounts, bids, terms of sale, customers or suppliers (other than in respect of the JV business as permitted by the Antitrust Compliance Annex), capacity, output, wages or other terms of employment, or any other competitively sensitive matter relating to the Parties’ respective businesses outside the Transaction. Any participant may terminate a discussion that he or she believes to be inappropriate, and such termination shall be recorded in the minutes.”")

H("Issue 7 — The Northwind Aerospace Bid (Critical; not addressed by the draft)", 3)
P("Pinnacle and Lakeshore are rival bidders on a three-year Northwind supply contract (~$22 million/year), with award expected in February 2025. If the NDA is signed January 31, § 6.1 would require the delivery of current pricing schedules, discount matrices and customer revenue data by about March 2, 2025 — during or immediately around the award decision. Lakeshore’s receipt of Pinnacle’s current aerospace pricing (or vice versa) while the bid is open, or while best-and-final or post-award negotiations remain possible, could be characterized as facilitating bid rigging (a per se, criminal offense) and would at minimum create a damaging evidentiary record if the losing bidder or Northwind later questioned the outcome. Aerospace pricing has no relevance to an automotive rCF JV.", align="j")
P("**Recommendations:**")
B("Add an express blackout: no Party shall request, disclose or discuss any information concerning the Northwind procurement or any other pending or anticipated bid, tender or RFQ in which both Parties are or may be participants, at any time, including after award.")
B("No Phase 2 (Clean Team) commercial or cost data should be exchanged before the Northwind award is announced and any best-and-final or negotiation round has concluded; Phase 1 technical rCF work can proceed.")
B("Instruct the Pinnacle Northwind bid team (in writing) that it must not receive any Project Meridian information, and confirm that no Northwind bid team member is on the Clean Team.")
B("Each party should confirm in writing (Annex) that its Northwind bid was and will be determined independently.")
B("If Pinnacle learns of any communication between the parties concerning Northwind, it should contact us immediately.")

H("Issue 8 — §§ 1.8 and 3.1 Transaction / Permitted Purpose (High)", 3)
P("“Transaction” and “Permitted Purpose” cover “any joint venture, merger, acquisition, licensing arrangement, or other business combination,” and include “consummating” the Transaction and “integration planning activities.” As your email notes, this is an M&A form. It is inconsistent with the Board-approved scope — a JV focused “exclusively” on rCF, with no consolidation of existing operations — and it broadens the legitimate need for information to whole-company merger diligence, which the parties would then use to justify existing-business data requests. “Consummating” and “integration planning” invite pre-closing implementation and coordination (gun-jumping). The definition is also duplicated (once in § 1.8 and again in § 3.1), which should be cleaned up.", align="j")
P("**Recommended revision:**")
Q("“‘Transaction’ means a potential joint venture between the Parties limited to the research, development, manufacture and commercialization of recycled carbon fiber products for automotive lightweighting applications (the ‘JV Business’). ‘Permitted Purpose’ means the evaluation and negotiation of the Transaction and, to the extent permitted by the Clean Team Agreement and Antitrust Compliance Annex, planning for the formation and operation of the JV Business following execution of definitive agreements. The Permitted Purpose does not include the implementation of any aspect of the Transaction, or any coordination of the Parties’ respective businesses, prior to the consummation of the Transaction and receipt of any required regulatory clearances.”")

H("Issue 9 — § 2.1 Confidential Information Definition (High)", 3)
P("From a confidentiality standpoint a broad definition is protective, and Pinnacle should not want its own information left unprotected merely because it falls outside rCF. The antitrust risk is not that the definition protects too much, but that §§ 2.1, 6.1 and 4.1 together presuppose and authorize the exchange of all of it, without any differentiated handling. Items (c) pricing, (d) customer lists/contracts/pricing/volumes, (e) supplier and raw material costs, (f) production volumes, capacity utilization and plant-level costs, (g) product roadmaps, (h) compensation data and (i) sales volumes and market share are all competitively sensitive. **Recommendation:** keep a broad definition of Confidential Information for protection purposes, but (i) add a defined subcategory of Competitively Sensitive Information (Appendix B, § 2.4) subject to clean team handling, (ii) require CSI to be labeled “CLEAN TEAM ONLY” or “OUTSIDE COUNSEL ONLY” (while preserving protection for unlabeled information), and (iii) add a statement that inclusion of a category in the definition does not imply that such information will be or should be exchanged. Also expressly cover information disclosed prior to the Effective Date in connection with Project Meridian, so any earlier executive-level discussions are protected.", align="j")

H("Issue 10 — § 2.1(h) Employee Compensation Data (High)", 3)
P("Pinnacle and Lakeshore compete for engineers, technicians and plant workers. The exchange of compensation and headcount data between competing employers carries wage-fixing risk that the agencies treat seriously (2025 Worker Guidelines; 2016 HR Guidance), and the Team Memo specifically contemplates exchanging “compensation benchmarking data for relevant technical and operational roles.” **Recommendation:** no exchange of individual or role-level compensation data between the parties. If JV staffing economics require it, use an independent compensation consultant to prepare aggregated, anonymized JV staffing cost assumptions, or exchange only aggregated data for specific individuals proposed to be seconded to the JV, through the Clean Team.", align="j")

H("Issue 11 — § 8.1 Term and Automatic Renewal (High)", 3)
P("The 18-month Initial Term automatically renews for successive 12-month periods unless either party gives 90 days’ notice. Because the term drives the Evaluation Period, the § 6.2 quarterly exchanges, the § 6.3 meetings and the start of the 24-month non-solicit and standstill tails, auto-renewal could perpetuate a recurring competitor data exchange indefinitely if neither party remembers to give notice. Prolonged exchange untethered to a live deal is hard to justify. **Recommendation:** fixed term of 12 months (comfortably covering the June 30, 2025 definitive agreement target), terminable by either party on written notice and terminating automatically on execution of definitive agreements (which will contain their own provisions) or termination of discussions; any extension only by written agreement. The five-year confidentiality survival in § 8.2 is appropriate and protective and may be retained; consider extending trade-secret protection for as long as the information remains a trade secret.", align="j")

H("Issue 12 — § 7.1 Employee Non-Solicitation (High)", 3)
P("Section 7.1 bars soliciting, recruiting, **or hiring** any employee (or former employee within six months) who became known in connection with the Transaction, for the term (auto-renewing) plus 24 months. A non-solicit ancillary to a legitimate JV evaluation is defensible if reasonably necessary and narrowly tailored, but this one has features that increase the risk of it being characterized as a no-poach agreement: (i) the “hire” prohibition operates as a no-hire restraint even for employees who apply on their own; (ii) its duration is open-ended because it runs from an auto-renewing term; (iii) “became known … in connection with the Transaction” is loosely defined and could sweep in large numbers of employees; and (iv) it covers former employees. **Recommendation:**", align="j")
Q("“7.1 For a period of twelve (12) months from the Effective Date, neither Party shall, directly or indirectly, solicit for employment any officer or employee of the other Party with whom it first had contact, or of whom it first became aware, through the evaluation of the Transaction; provided that this Section 7.1 shall not restrict (a) general solicitations (including through search firms) not specifically directed at such persons, or hiring persons who respond thereto, (b) soliciting or hiring any person who first contacts the soliciting Party on his or her own initiative, or (c) soliciting or hiring any person whose employment was terminated by the other Party.”")
P("We also recommend confirming whether the parties have Canadian employees, given Canada’s criminal no-poach provision.", align="j")

H("Issue 13 — § 5.2 Exclusions; Absence of Compelled/Regulatory Disclosure Clause (Medium)", 3)
P("The exclusions omit two standard carve-outs that have particular antitrust importance between competitors: (i) information **independently developed** without use of the other’s Confidential Information, and (ii) information **received from a third party** without a duty of confidentiality. Without them, Pinnacle could face claims that its own independently developed pricing, product or rCF strategy was “derived from” Lakeshore information, which chills independent competition. The written-records requirement in § 5.2(b) should be relaxed to “as shown by competent evidence.” Separately, the NDA has no provision permitting disclosure required by law or requested by a governmental authority. Pinnacle must be free to respond to an HSR filing requirement, a Second Request, a civil investigative demand, a subpoena or an informal agency inquiry without breaching the NDA, and should not be required to give the other party advance notice of a confidential governmental antitrust inquiry where that is prohibited or inappropriate. See Appendix B, §§ 5.2 and 5.4.", align="j")

H("Issue 14 — §§ 12.9, 12.10 No Independence or Antitrust Compliance Clause (Medium)", 3)
P("The general “Compliance with Law” clause in § 12.10 is not sufficient. The NDA should affirmatively record that (i) the parties are and will remain independent competitors; (ii) nothing in the Agreement requires or permits any agreement on prices, output, customers, territories, bids, wages or other competitive matters; (iii) each party will continue to make its own competitive decisions independently; (iv) either party may decline to provide information on antitrust grounds; and (v) the Clean Team Agreement and Antitrust Compliance Annex control in case of conflict. This clause is useful both as a behavioral guide and as contemporaneous evidence of the parties’ intent. See Appendix B, § 12.11.", align="j")

H("Issue 15 — § 8.3 Return or Destruction (Medium)", 3)
P("Section 8.3 allows retention of one archival copy without specifying who holds it, and exempts Residual Information. **Recommendation:** archival copies (and copies retained on automatic backup systems) to be held only by the legal department or outside counsel and accessible only for compliance and enforcement; delete clause (ii); require Clean Team materials and Derivative Materials containing CSI to be destroyed with written certification by a Clean Team member and counsel; confirm the obligation survives.", align="j")

H("Issues 16–20 — Lower-severity points", 3)
B("**§ 4.3 Information Access Log (retain and strengthen).** This is a positive feature that supports compliance and should be retained. Expand it to record, for CSI, each Clean Team member granted access, the date and the materials accessed, and integrate it with the virtual data room’s access logs.")
B("**§ 2.3 Derivative Materials.** Appropriate as a protective matter. Add a mechanism under which Clean Team members and outside advisers may prepare summaries that aggregate or sanitize CSI and, once cleared by outside antitrust counsel for the producing party, share them with the broader evaluation team.")
B("**§ 7.2 Standstill.** Standstills raise limited antitrust risk. Clarify that clause (a) does not restrict ordinary-course purchases of products or assets; shorten the tail to 12 months; add a customary fall-away if a third party announces or makes an offer for a party; and confirm whether either party has registered securities (§ 13(d) references suggest a public-company form; Lakeshore is an LLC).")
B("**§§ 9.1, 9.2 Governing Law/Arbitration.** Not antitrust issues as such, but: the National Arbitration Forum withdrew from consumer arbitration in 2009 and its suitability as an administrator for a commercial dispute should be confirmed — we recommend AAA (Commercial Rules) or JAMS; preserve the right to seek interim injunctive relief in court (consistent with § 10.1); and consider Delaware law (both parties are Delaware entities) as a neutral alternative to Ohio, Lakeshore’s home state.")
B("**§ 12.1 Entire Agreement.** Ensure the Clean Team Agreement and Antitrust Compliance Annex are attached as exhibits, are expressly incorporated, prevail over any conflicting NDA provision, and survive termination.")

H("VI. Clean Team Protocol and Antitrust Compliance Annex — Recommendation", 1)
P("**Recommendation: both, and as a condition of the NDA rather than a supplement.** Pinnacle should require (i) a Clean Team Agreement governing who may access Competitively Sensitive Information and how, and (ii) an Antitrust Compliance Annex governing the conduct of the evaluation (communications, meetings, documents, bid blackout, integration planning limits). Both should be exhibits to and incorporated into the NDA, should prevail over the NDA body in case of conflict, and execution of both (plus designation and training of Clean Team members) should be an express condition precedent to any exchange of information beyond Phase 1 non-sensitive material. Putting these in a side letter or leaving them to be negotiated later would risk the exchange beginning before the safeguards exist, and the § 12.1 integration clause could undercut a separate document. A key term sheet is at Appendix A.", align="j")
P("**Why it matters here.** Clean teams are the standard tool for competitor diligence and are expected by the agencies. They allow the legitimate evaluation to proceed — the CFO and CTO can assess JV economics and technology — while keeping a competitor’s pricing and customer intelligence away from the people who compete against it. A properly designed, documented and followed clean team process is also Pinnacle’s best evidence, if ever asked, that it met the Board’s safeguards condition.", align="j")

H("VII. The Northwind Bid — Practical Steps", 1)
P("In addition to the contractual blackout (Issue 7): (1) identify the Northwind bid team in writing and wall it off from Project Meridian; (2) defer any Tier 2/Tier 3 exchange until the Northwind award has been made and any negotiations concluded; (3) instruct all evaluation team members not to mention Northwind or any customer procurement in communications with Lakeshore; (4) document the date and basis of Pinnacle’s final Northwind pricing and keep that record; and (5) if the award goes to Lakeshore, avoid internal commentary linking the result to Project Meridian. The same blackout should apply to any other procurement in which both parties are competing.", align="j")

H("VIII. Negotiation Strategy and Timeline", 1)
P("**Non-negotiable (do not sign without):** deletion of §§ 5.3/1.7/8.3(ii) and 9.3; deletion of the mandatory and recurring exchange in §§ 6.1–6.2; a clean team and need-to-know restriction; restructured meetings in § 6.3; the Northwind/bid blackout; narrowing of the Transaction to the rCF JV; deletion of auto-renewal; and the compelled/regulatory disclosure clause.", align="j")
P("**Important but negotiable:** non-solicit duration and carve-outs; standstill details; governing law and arbitral institution; archival copy mechanics; exact Clean Team membership (Lakeshore will propose its own list, which Pinnacle should also review to ensure Lakeshore’s sales and pricing personnel are excluded).", align="j")
P("**Framing.** These revisions protect both parties equally and Lakeshore’s counsel should recognize them as market-standard for competitor transactions; the existing draft exposes Lakeshore as much as Pinnacle. We recommend presenting the changes as necessary to satisfy Pinnacle’s Board condition and to protect the JV’s eventual regulatory review, rather than as a criticism of HDM’s draft. We would avoid any written suggestion that the original draft was “illegal”; the redline speaks for itself.", align="j")

**MEMORANDUM**

  ----------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **TO:**                             David Yoon, General Counsel, Pinnacle Fiber Technologies, Inc.

  **FROM:**                           Catherine (Kate) Ellsworth, Partner; James Okoro, Associate --- Westbrook & Calloway LLP

  **DATE:**                           January 21, 2025

  **RE:**                             Project Meridian --- Antitrust and Competition Law Review of Lakeshore's Draft Mutual Confidentiality and Non-Disclosure Agreement (Hargrove Dean & Millstein draft dated January 10, 2025); Recommended Revisions; Clean Team Protocol and Antitrust Compliance Annex
  ----------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# I. Executive Summary (suitable for sharing with Ms. Thornton and the Board)

**Bottom line.** The Lakeshore draft NDA should not be signed in its current form. It is a general-purpose M&A confidentiality agreement that, as drafted, would require two direct horizontal competitors --- the #1 (Lakeshore, \~19%) and #3 (Pinnacle, \~14%) producers in the North American carbon fiber reinforcement market --- to exchange, on a mandatory and recurring basis, the most competitively sensitive information in their existing virgin carbon fiber businesses (current pricing schedules, discount matrices, customer-by-customer revenue, plant-level capacity utilization and five-year strategic plans), and to do so with no clean team, no firewall, no counsel oversight and no limitation to the actual subject of the deal: a greenfield 50/50 joint venture limited to recycled carbon fiber (rCF) for automotive lightweighting. Several provisions would, in our view, create meaningful exposure under Section 1 of the Sherman Act and would be difficult to explain to the DOJ Antitrust Division or the FTC if the information exchange or the JV were ever investigated.

**The problems are fixable, and the transaction itself can proceed.** Competitor collaborations to develop a new product are common and lawful when the information exchanged is limited to what is reasonably necessary to evaluate the collaboration and is handled through appropriate safeguards. With the revisions below, Pinnacle can satisfy the Board's condition that "appropriate antitrust safeguards" be in place before anything is executed.

**Most significant issues (all rated Critical):**

- **Mandatory and recurring exchange of competitively sensitive information (§§ 6.1, 6.2).** The required deliverables --- current pricing schedules and discount matrices, customer lists with revenue by customer, capacity and utilization by facility, product-line margins and five-year strategic plans, refreshed quarterly for 18+ months --- go far beyond what is needed to evaluate an rCF JV in which neither party has a product. A standing, periodic exchange of current, disaggregated price and output data between leading competitors is the classic fact pattern for an unlawful information exchange.

- **No clean team or firewall (§§ 1.6, 4.1).** Confidential Information may go to any "Representative," including affiliates and all employees, at the recipient's sole discretion. Pinnacle's VP of Sales (Brian Hecht) and VP of Strategic Pricing (Elena Vasquez), who set competitive prices daily, would have unrestricted access to Lakeshore's pricing and customer data.

- **Residuals clause (§§ 1.7, 5.3, 8.3(ii)).** Each party may freely use in its business whatever its people remember of the other's Confidential Information --- in practice, a contractual license to use a competitor's pricing and customer intelligence in competition. It must be deleted.

- **Waiver of antitrust claims (§ 9.3).** A prospective release of antitrust and unfair competition claims arising from the exchange is very likely unenforceable as against public policy, cannot bind the government or customers, strips Pinnacle of protection if Lakeshore misuses Pinnacle data, and --- most importantly --- reads as an acknowledgment that the parties anticipated anticompetitive conduct. It must be deleted.

- **Monthly senior-executive meetings on "matters of mutual interest" (§ 6.3)** with no agenda, counsel or scope limits --- an open channel between competing executives.

- **The pending Northwind Aerospace bid.** Pinnacle and Lakeshore are competing bidders for a \~\$22 million/year, three-year Northwind supply contract to be awarded in February 2025 --- exactly when the NDA's 30-day mandatory exchange of current pricing and customer data would occur. Any exchange touching that bid risks being characterized as bid rigging, which is a per se, criminally prosecuted offense.
